What We're Serving

The Night's
Menu

Sourced daily. Market-driven.
Prepared by hand.
Menu shifts with the tides.

Raw Bar

Oyster Tray

$18

Half-dozen freshly shucked Johns Island oysters on the half shell — briny, cold, and clean as the tide. Served with house mignonette, fresh horseradish, and a wedge of lemon.

Peel-and-Eat Shrimp

$16

One pound of wild-caught Lowcountry shrimp, steamed in Old Bay and sea salt. Served with house lemon aioli and house cocktail sauce. Peel it. Dip it. There's your evening.

From the Kitchen

Crab Rice Fritters

$14

Blue crab folded into Carolina gold rice, pan-crisped until burnished and served with a smoked paprika remoulade. A Lowcountry staple done the way it always should've been.

Blackened Local Catch

$24

Today's fish — flounder, sheepshead, or whatever the boats brought in — hit with Nate's spice blend and seared in a screaming-hot cast iron. Herb butter, lemon, cucumber-tomato relish.

Hushpuppies

$7

Golden-fried cornmeal fritters with scallion and a whisper of jalapeño. Crisp shell, pillowy inside. You'll order a second basket before the first one is gone. We already know.

Tomato Cucumber Salad

$9

Peak-season tomatoes and garden cucumbers in a white balsamic vinaigrette with fresh dill, shaved red onion, and flaky salt. Bright, sharp, and exactly what you need alongside the rest of this.

To Finish

Key Lime Pie Jars

$8

Tart key lime curd layered over a buttery graham cracker crumble, finished with whipped cream and lime zest. Punchy. Creamy. The exact right note to end on.

Rotating Spritz

$11

Tonight: Aperol, blood orange, and soda with a rosemary sprig and orange peel. Changes with the season and Nate's mood. Always cold. Always worth asking about.

Chef Nate Rivers
Charleston-born. Dock-raised.

The Story

About
Nate Rivers

"The best meal I ever had was standing at a folding table on my uncle's dock. I've been trying to recreate that ever since."

Nate Rivers grew up in North Charleston with a grandfather who cast nets before sunrise and a grandmother who could take a pound of blue crab and turn it into something you'd still be talking about a decade later. He didn't go to culinary school right away — he worked the docks first, then the kitchens of other people's restaurants, before he felt ready enough to own the whole thing.

Low Tide Table started as a way to get back to what mattered: seasonal, local seafood prepared simply and served the way Lowcountry cooking always has been — without fuss, without pretense, with a cold drink in hand and the smell of salt in the air.

Every Thursday through Saturday evening, Nate and a small crew set up at The Dockyard Courtyard with whatever came off the boats that morning. The menu is short on purpose. Everything is made from scratch, every time, in a space where the air still carries the tides.
